title: What are common chaos experiments — kill a random pod/container, add network latency between services, fill disk space, simulate database failure, block a dependency — and what should happen (graceful degradation, not total failure)?
shortTitle: Common chaos experiments and the expected graceful behavior

s1_definition.profdef: Common chaos experiments inject specific, realistic faults to test particular resilience mechanisms: killing a random pod or container to test failover and self-healing, adding network latency or packet loss between services to test timeouts and retries, filling disk space to test resource-exhaustion handling, simulating a database failure to test fallback and recovery, and blocking a dependency to test circuit breakers and graceful degradation. In every case the expected outcome is graceful degradation, the system continues to serve, perhaps in a reduced capacity, rather than failing totally, and it recovers when the fault is removed.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, each chaos experiment pokes a different weak spot to check the system bends instead of breaking. Killing a random server checks another one takes over so customers never notice. Slowing the network checks the system waits sensibly and retries instead of hanging forever. Filling the disk checks the system handles running out of space without corrupting data. Simulating the database going down checks the app shows a polite "try again shortly" and recovers, rather than crashing. Blocking a dependency, say the fraud-check service, checks the app degrades gracefully, maybe queueing or safely declining, instead of taking the whole bank down. The common thread is that a single failure should cause a controlled, limited degradation, never a total outage.
s1_definition.oneliner: Common chaos experiments kill a pod to test failover, add network latency to test timeouts and retries, fill disk to test resource handling, simulate database failure to test fallback and recovery, and block a dependency to test circuit breakers, and in every case the system should degrade gracefully, not fail totally.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Common chaos experiments inject specific, realistic faults to test particular resilience mechanisms: killing a random pod or container to test failover and self-healing, adding network latency or packet loss between services to test timeouts and retries, filling disk space to test resource-exhaustion handling, simulating a database failure to test fallback and recovery, and blocking a dependency to test circuit breakers and graceful degradation. In every case the expected outcome is graceful degradation, the system continues to serve, perhaps in a reduced capacity, rather than failing totally, and it recovers when the fault is removed.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, each chaos experiment pokes a different weak spot to check the system bends instead of breaking. Killing a random server checks another one takes over so customers never notice. Slowing the network checks the system waits sensibly and retries instead of hanging forever. Filling the disk checks the system handles running out of space without corrupting data. Simulating the database going down checks the app shows a polite "try again shortly" and recovers, rather than crashing. Blocking a dependency, say the fraud-check service, checks the app degrades gracefully, maybe queueing or safely declining, instead of taking the whole bank down. The common thread is that a single failure should cause a controlled, limited degradation, never a total outage.

**One line to remember:** Common chaos experiments kill a pod to test failover, add network latency to test timeouts and retries, fill disk to test resource handling, simulate database failure to test fallback and recovery, and block a dependency to test circuit breakers, and in every case the system should degrade gracefully, not fail totally.

sections.s2_technical:
Each experiment targets a distinct failure mode and a distinct resilience mechanism, and each has an expected graceful behavior. Killing a random pod or container tests self-healing and failover: in a healthy system the orchestrator detects the lost instance, the load balancer stops routing to it, traffic shifts to healthy instances, and the orchestrator starts a replacement, so the steady-state success rate barely moves. The failure mode it catches is a single point of failure or missing redundancy where losing one instance drops requests. Adding network latency or packet loss between services tests timeout and retry configuration: the system should have sensible timeouts so a slow dependency does not cause unbounded waiting, bounded retries with backoff so it recovers without amplifying load, and bulkheads so one slow path does not exhaust all threads. The failure mode it catches is a missing or overly long timeout that makes a slow dependency hang the whole service, or a naive retry that creates a retry storm.

Filling disk space tests resource-exhaustion handling: the system should fail safely, for example rejecting new writes cleanly, rotating or shedding logs, and alerting, rather than corrupting data or crashing unpredictably. The failure mode it catches is unbounded log or temp growth and no monitoring, which in production silently fills a disk and brings a node down. Simulating a database failure, taking the database or its connection down, tests fallback, degradation, and recovery: the system should return clear errors or serve from a cache where safe, should not crash, should back off and reconnect when the database returns, and must never lose or corrupt committed data. The failure mode it catches is a service that crashes or hangs when its database blips, or one that loses data on reconnect. Blocking a dependency, making a downstream service unreachable or time out, tests the circuit breaker and graceful degradation: the circuit should open after repeated failures so calls fail fast instead of piling up, a fallback should provide a safe default or a queued path, and the rest of the system should keep working. The failure mode it catches is a cascading failure where one unhealthy dependency drags down everything that calls it.

The unifying expectation is graceful degradation rather than total failure. A resilient system responds to a single component failure with a controlled, bounded reduction in capability, failover, fast-failing with fallbacks, clear user-facing errors, and automatic recovery, so customers experience at worst a minor, temporary impact instead of an outage. When an experiment instead produces a total failure or a cascade, you have found exactly the weakness to fix, add the timeout, size the pool, configure the circuit breaker, add the fallback, fix the retry policy, or add redundancy, before it happens for real.

The senior nuances are that each experiment should be tied to a specific hypothesis about a specific mechanism, not run blindly, and that you escalate from non-production to a small production blast radius with monitoring and an abort. You pair each experiment with the resilience pattern it validates, failover, timeouts and bounded retries, resource limits and shedding, caching and reconnection, circuit breakers and fallbacks, so a failed experiment points directly at the fix. You also test recovery, not just failure, confirming the system returns to steady state when the fault is removed, because partial recovery or stuck states are common bugs. In a bank you are especially careful to design experiments that never risk financial data integrity, so you simulate a database being unreachable rather than deleting data, and you verify that committed transactions survive and that the system degrades to safe behavior, declining or queuing rather than double-processing. The outcome of a mature chaos program is a system where killing a pod, slowing a link, filling a disk, dropping the database, or blocking a dependency each produces a small, well-understood, recoverable degradation that you have already seen and handled, so real incidents during peaks like salary day are non-events.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India must verify that each of several faults produces graceful degradation, not a total outage, so it runs a suite of experiments each tied to a resilience mechanism. This is exactly the common-experiments-to-expected-behavior mapping.

Problem 2 — Blocking the fraud-check dependency must open a circuit breaker and use a safe fallback rather than cascading, and a database failure must degrade and recover, not crash or lose data. These are exactly the per-fault expected behaviors.

Problem 3 — Any experiment that produces total failure reveals the weakness and the fix. This is exactly learning the resilience gap.

In the mini-project we build a chaos suite that injects each fault into a resilient service model and checks whether the response is graceful degradation or total failure, mapping each experiment to its expected behavior. We write a Java harness.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a fully resilient service with failover, timeouts, disk-full handling, database fallback, and a circuit breaker, and a fragile service missing the database fallback and circuit breaker.

Step 1: The suite injects kill-pod into the resilient service, which reroutes to healthy instances while the orchestrator restarts the pod, so the behavior is graceful degradation and the experiment passes.

Step 2: It injects network latency, and because the service has timeouts and bounded retries with backoff and bulkheads, slowness is isolated rather than hanging the service, again graceful.

Step 3: It injects fill-disk and database-failure into the resilient service, which rejects new writes cleanly and alerts for the disk, and returns clear errors or cache reads and reconnects without data loss for the database, both graceful and recoverable.

Step 4: It injects block-dependency into the resilient service, whose circuit breaker opens to fail fast with a safe fallback so there is no cascade, graceful.

Step 5: The suite then injects the database failure and blocked dependency into the fragile service, which lacks the fallback and circuit breaker, so both produce total failure, a crash on the database blip and a cascading failure from the blocked dependency, and the demo flags each as a weakness to fix, demonstrating that the expected outcome everywhere is graceful degradation and that a total failure pinpoints the missing resilience pattern.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The common chaos experiments each target a distinct failure mode and the resilience mechanism that should handle it, and in every case the expected outcome is graceful degradation, not total failure. Killing a random pod or container tests self-healing and failover: the orchestrator should detect the loss, the load balancer should stop routing to it, traffic should shift to healthy instances, and a replacement should start, so the success rate barely moves. Adding network latency or packet loss between services tests timeouts and retries: the service should have sensible timeouts so a slow dependency does not hang it, bounded retries with backoff so it does not create a retry storm, and bulkheads so one slow path does not exhaust all threads. Filling disk space tests resource-exhaustion handling: the system should reject new writes cleanly, shed or rotate logs, and alert, rather than corrupting data or crashing. Simulating a database failure tests fallback and recovery: the service should return clear errors or serve safe cache reads, back off and reconnect when the database returns, and never lose committed data. And blocking a dependency tests the circuit breaker and graceful degradation: the circuit should open after repeated failures so calls fail fast with a safe fallback, and the rest of the system should keep working rather than cascading into a total outage.

The unifying expectation is that a single component failure produces a controlled, bounded reduction in capability, failover, fast-failing with fallbacks, clear user-facing errors, and automatic recovery, so customers experience at worst a minor temporary impact. When an experiment instead produces a total failure or a cascade, I have found exactly the weakness to fix, the missing timeout, the unsized pool, the absent circuit breaker, the missing fallback, the naive retry, or the lack of redundancy, before it happens for real. I also always verify recovery, not just failure, because stuck or partial-recovery states are common bugs.

At the National Bank of India I ran exactly this suite. Killing a transfer pod rerouted cleanly, adding latency to the fraud-check call was absorbed by timeouts and a bulkhead, but blocking the fraud dependency on one service revealed there was no circuit breaker, so calls piled up and it cascaded, a total failure we only saw because we injected it deliberately, and we fixed it by adding a circuit breaker and a safe fallback that declined conservatively. I designed every database experiment to simulate unreachability rather than touch data, so financial integrity was never at risk. Being able to map each common experiment, kill a pod, add latency, fill disk, fail the database, block a dependency, to the mechanism it tests and to the expected graceful behavior, and to say that a total failure pinpoints the fix, is what shows an interviewer I understand chaos experiments as targeted resilience verification whose goal is bend, not break.
